passages.happening:
With the land divided, the LORD speaks to Joshua about something Moses had already commanded. “Tell the Israelites to designate the cities of refuge, as I instructed you through Moses, so that anyone who kills another unintentionally or accidentally may flee there. These will be your refuge from the avenger of blood” (verses 2-3).

He sets out how it is to work. The person who flees comes to the gate of one of these cities and states his case to the elders. They are to take him in and give him a place to live among them (verse 4). If the avenger of blood comes after him, they must not hand him over, ‘because that man killed his neighbor accidentally without prior malice’ (verse 5).

He is to stay there until he has stood trial before the assembly, and until the death of the high priest serving at that time. “Then the manslayer may return to his own home in the city from which he fled” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
To understand this law a reader has to picture a world with no police, no public prosecutor and no prisons. When someone was killed, it fell to the dead person's family to see justice done. The nearest male relative had the duty. He was called the avenger of blood.

That system held murder in check, because a killer knew that someone would come for him. But it had a terrible weakness. A grieving relative does not stop to ask whether the death was meant. A man whose axe head flew off and struck his neighbor could be hunted down and killed before anyone heard what had happened. And one killing could become a feud that ran for generations.

The cities of refuge were God's limit on this. They did two things. They drew a clear line between murder and accident, and they put a hearing between the death and any punishment. The man who fled was safe until his case was heard. If the assembly found that he had killed on purpose, the city gave him no shelter. If it found that the death was an accident, the avenger could not touch him.

The city gate was where the elders of a town sat to hear cases. The fugitive had to tell his story there first. The Hebrew word for ‘refuge’ means a place where one is taken in. It was not a hole to hide in. The man had to be received by a community and given somewhere to live.

Even an accidental killing was not treated as nothing. The man had to leave his home and live in the city of refuge, perhaps for many years. A life had been lost, and the law marked that. The Hebrew uses for his act the same verb as the commandment against murder. Every death was serious. The judgment depended on intent.

His release came with the death of the high priest. The text does not say why.

This was a law for ancient Israel, in a society where families avenged their dead. The role of the avenger of blood belonged to a world without police or public courts. Nothing here permits any family or any person today to take revenge for a death. Where the law points is the other way, toward a fair hearing before any penalty.
passages.later:
Moses gave the plainest example of the kind of case the law had in mind. A man goes into the forest with his neighbor to cut wood, ‘and swings his axe to chop down a tree, but the blade flies off the handle and strikes and kills his neighbor’. Such a man ‘may flee to one of these cities to save his life’ (Deuteronomy 19:5).

The letter to the Hebrews borrows the picture of running to a place of safety and uses it of Christian hope: ‘we who have fled to take hold of the hope set before us may be strongly encouraged’ (Hebrews 6:18). It goes on to speak of Jesus as ‘a high priest forever’ (Hebrews 6:20). The New Testament does not call Christ a city of refuge, though Christian readers have long drawn the comparison.
passages.asks: This law put a hearing between a death and the anger of those who grieved. Ask whether you are quick to judge when you have heard only one side, or when you are hurt. Ask who needs you to slow down and listen to the whole story. And if you are the one who needs somewhere to run, ask whether you have told your case plainly to God, who takes people in.

passages.t: Six cities, within reach of everyone
passages.happening:
Israel names the cities. West of the Jordan there are three: “Kedesh in Galilee in the hill country of Naphtali, Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim, and Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron) in the hill country of Judah” (verse 7).

East of the Jordan there are three more: Bezer on the plateau, from the tribe of Reuben; Ramoth in Gilead, from Gad; and Golan in Bashan, from Manasseh (verse 8).

The chapter closes by saying whom they were for. “These are the cities appointed for all the Israelites and foreigners among them, so that anyone who kills a person unintentionally may flee there and not die by the hand of the avenger of blood prior to standing trial before the assembly” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
The six cities are set out with care. On each side of the river there is one in the north, one in the middle and one in the south. Wherever a person lived in Israel, one of them was within reach. A place of safety that could not be reached in time would have been no safety.

Several of them were old and honored towns. Shechem was where Abraham first built an altar in the land. Hebron had been Abraham's home and was now Caleb's. All six were also towns of the Levites, as the next chapter shows. The people who knew the law best lived where the hardest cases would arrive.

The last verse says the cities were for ‘all the Israelites and foreigners among them’. The protection did not depend on being born an Israelite. A foreigner living in the land who killed someone by accident had the same right to run and the same right to be heard.

The Old Testament does not record any case of a person using one of these cities. Later Jewish teaching discussed the law in close detail. What the chapter shows is what kind of society God told Israel to be. It was to be one in which anger did not have the last word, and in which even a stranger could count on a hearing.
passages.later:
Moses gave the reason for the whole provision: “Thus innocent blood will not be shed in the land that the LORD your God is giving you as an inheritance, so that you will not be guilty of bloodshed” (Deuteronomy 19:10).

The law of Moses held the foreigner and the native to one standard in such matters: “You are to have the same standard of law for the foreign resident and the native; for I am the LORD your God” (Leviticus 24:22).
passages.asks: The cities were spread so that no one was too far from safety, and they were open to the foreigner as well. Ask who in your town has nowhere to turn when things go wrong. Ask whether your church or your home is a place a frightened person could reach in time, and whether a stranger would be taken in as readily as one of your own.
